results.summary_before: This project implements a 4-bit digital lock that asserts an UNLOCK output when the input code equals 1011. Three additional outputs act as Easter eggs for the near-miss codes 1010, 1001 and 0011, and all outputs stay low for any other code. Testing is done by toggling the four input switches and observing LEDs or a 7-segment display against the supplied truth table. The design is a small combinational pattern matcher with clear documentation and no external hardware requirements.

results.summary_before: This is a spiking pattern recognition core based on a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that triggers an event when a target spike pattern is detected. It uses input switches to set the pattern and a signal generator to provide a 0.5Hz square wave. When the pattern matches, an output drives a MOSFET module to rotate a motor. The clock is deliberately set to 2 Hz to make internal processing observable, and the design is intended for educational demonstrations of robotic reflex responses.

results.summary_before: This design plots the trajectory of a fixed system of two ordinary differential equations on a VGA display, using the coefficients a=0, b=-1, c=1, d=0. A reset transition from low to high starts the plotting, and cycling the reset restarts the trace from the beginning. It requires a 25 MHz clock and a Tiny VGA PMOD connected to the output header. The author describes it as a very bad and very unstable plotter, and the documentation does not cover any silicon test results.

results.summary_before: Tiny Canvas is a hardware drawing tool that mimics MS Paint, controlled by an SNES-compatible gamepad and outputting canvas coordinates and color data over I2C. It supports RGB color mixing, variable brush sizes, symmetry modes, and fill rectangle operations. The design requires a Gamepad PMOD and an SNES controller, and an I2C master device to render the canvas on a display. It is a 1x1 tile design that streams paint events in real-time to a host for a 256x256 canvas.

results.summary_before: The VGA Clock Demo is a Verilog design that renders a circular analog clock face on a 640x480 VGA display, with background colors and sun/moon positions changing based on the time of day. It includes hour, minute, and second hands, and allows time adjustment via a Gamepad PMOD. The clock starts at 00:00:00 and can be set using the gamepad buttons. It requires a VGA monitor and a Gamepad PMOD, and is notable for its visual representation of time with day/night themes.
